result.summary: Pausanias describes the springs of the river Ladon in Arcadia, noting a report that they are fed from the marsh at Pheneus. He then recounts the Arcadian and Elean story of Leucippus, who disguised himself as a girl to win Daphne and was killed when his sex was discovered.

scenes.title: The springs of the Ladon
scenes.summary: Pausanias travels about 50 stades from Lycuria to the springs of the Ladon. He doubts the report that the water comes from the Pheneus marsh, and praises the river's beauty.

scenes.title: Leucippus disguised for Daphne
scenes.summary: Leucippus, son of Oenomaus, dresses as a girl to win Daphne's friendship. Apollo, jealous, is said to have caused his exposure, and the maidens killed him when he was found out while bathing in the Ladon.
scenes.stakes: Leucippus risks his life by deceiving Daphne and her companions.

analysis.text: The passage ties a landscape feature to myth, showing Pausanias's habit of pairing local geography with traditional stories while stating his doubts.
Pausanias notes rival local traditions about Daphne, Arcadian and Elean versus those along the Orontes, showing how myths varied by region.

legacy.text: The Leucippus and Daphne tale is a variant of the Daphne myth later retold in Ovid-style tradition with Apollo pursuing her, and by Parthenius and others.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias repeats the report that the Pheneus marsh water reappears at the Ladon springs but declines to confirm it, a common feature of Greek underground-drainage (karst) lore.

language_notes.text: A stade was a Greek unit of about 600 feet (roughly 180 metres), so 50 stades is about six miles.
Pausanias reports an underground-channel theory: water swallowed by pits (katavothra) in the mountains is said to resurface elsewhere, a common feature of Arcadia's limestone terrain.
The Orontes is a Syrian river; Antioch's Daphne story differs, with Daphne turned into a laurel, a version Pausanias declines to retell.
'Enamoured' means in love; 'hotly wooed' means ardently courted.
Growing hair 'to the Alpheus' means he dedicated it to the river Alpheus, a custom of youths; here he instead uses it to pass as a girl.

context_notes.text: Œnomaus, king of Pisa in Elis, is known for killing suitors of his daughter Hippodamia in chariot races; Leucippus is his son here.
Apollo was the god pursuing Daphne in the better-known myth, which ends with her becoming a laurel tree; here he is a jealous rival.
Daphne and her companions are huntresses devoted to chastity, like followers of Artemis, which explains their violent reaction to a male intruder.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a travelling observer, mixing personal aesthetic judgement with poetic fame to introduce the river's legend.
A suitor wins a man-hating girl's trust by disguising himself as a woman, turning her aversion into the means of intimacy.
The river bath meant to deepen friendship becomes the moment of exposure; the intimacy he gained leads directly to his death.
The curt closing formula distances Pausanias from the tale, signalling that he reports tradition without vouching for it.
